## Gainesville tornado
Illustration: Quartz
An EF-4 tornado that hit Gainesville, Georgia, on April 6, 1936, killed 203 people and injured 1,600 more. Among the 10 events on the list, only the Tri-State Tornado of 1925 left more people hurt. Georgia appears nowhere else in the table, which leaves this storm as the state's sole entry.
Gainesville's wounded outnumber those of every EF-5 storm in the table except Tri-State. The Georgia tornado carried an EF-4 estimate, one step below Joplin, Woodward$WWD -1.90%, and Flint, yet it harmed at least 600 more people than any of the three.
Gainesville also surpassed the two other EF-4 entries, the Great St. Louis Tornado and the Amite and Purvis tornado, in injuries. A lower intensity estimate did not cap how many people a storm on this list would harm. The table offers no reason for the gap, but it shows that a storm's estimated strength and its human toll did not rise in step.
Gainesville recorded about eight injuries for every death, the steepest such ratio in the table. Flint comes nearest at a little more than seven, and Joplin follows at about six. Tri-State, with far larger totals, left fewer than three injured for each person killed. Close to nine in 10 of the Georgia storm's recorded casualties survived.
Gainesville's 1,803 combined dead and injured trail only Tri-State's 2,722. No other event reached 1,300, including the Woodward Tornado, which crossed three states, and the Great St. Louis Tornado, which crossed two. A storm the table assigns to a single state outdid both. A multistate path on this list did not guarantee the heavier human cost.
Gainesville's combined toll also exceeds those of the Great Natchez Tornado, the Great St. Louis Tornado, and the Tupelo tornado, all three of which killed more people. A ranking built on deaths alone understates how many lives the Georgia storm upended.

## Tupelo tornado
Illustration: Quartz
An EF-5 tornado killed 216 people in Tupelo, Mississippi, on April 5, 1936, a toll that holds fourth place among the country's deadliest documented twisters. Of the six storms on the list carrying an EF-5 estimate, only the Tri-State Tornado claimed more lives. No event confined to a single state killed more people than the Tupelo storm. The Gainesville, Joplin, New Richmond, and Flint storms each hit one state, and each left a smaller death count. Tupelo's figure exceeds Joplin's by 58 deaths, a gap separating two EF-5 strikes 75 years apart.
Tupelo recorded 700 injuries, the second-smallest figure among the EF-5 entries and above only New Richmond's in Wisconsin. The Mississippi storm produced about 3.2 injuries per death, a lower ratio than six of the other nine events on the list. Only the Tri-State, Great Natchez, and New Richmond tornadoes left fewer wounded for each person killed. Tupelo's deaths weighed heavier against its injuries than at most other sites on the list.
Gainesville, Georgia, faced its own killer tornado the next day, April 6, 1936. Together, the two strikes on consecutive days claimed 419 lives, more than any single event on the list except the Tri-State Tornado. Their combined 2,300 injuries surpass the figure for every individual entry, Tri-State included. The pair also belongs to a wider April cluster. Four of the 10 events arrived in that month, including the Amite and Purvis storm of 1908 and the 1947 Woodward$WWD -1.90% Tornado, and no other month accounts for more than three.
Mississippi appears in three of the 10 entries, matching Missouri and outpacing every other state. The Great Natchez Tornado of 1840 and the Amite and Purvis event of 1908 each also reached Louisiana. Tupelo stands as the only one of the three confined to Mississippi. Spread across 96 years, from 1840 to 1936, those appearances show catastrophic tornadoes returning to the state across generations.

## Great St. Louis Tornado
Illustration: Quartz
The Great St. Louis Tornado killed 255 people and injured 1,000 more on May 27, 1896, as it moved across Missouri and Illinois. Its toll tops the two other EF-4 events in the table, the tornadoes that hit Gainesville and the towns of Amite and Purvis. Five of the six EF-5 storms on the list killed fewer people than this 1896 tornado did. Among the top-rated events, only the Tri-State Tornado took more lives, and its losses ran more than twice as heavy.
The tornado went by a second name, the Great Cyclone, and it cut into the center of St. Louis. Its path ran through the Soulard neighborhood and reached the levee downtown. Along the wharf, the funnel battered steamboats and ferryboats. The twister crossed the Mississippi River and inflicted heavy damage on the eastern approach of the Eads Bridge. From there it pushed into East St. Louis, Illinois, the other state on its listing.
The St. Louis tornado's injury count equals the one Joplin recorded in 2011, more than a century later. Only two entries wounded more people, the Tri-State Tornado and the Gainesville storm. No EF-5 event besides the Tri-State Tornado hurt more people than the 1896 storm. The 1896 tornado came 29 years before any of the three other events with four-digit injury tolls.
Only the 1840 Natchez tornado predates this one, and with Natchez unrated, the St. Louis twister stands as the oldest event in the table to carry an intensity estimate. Missouri and Mississippi each appear in three entries, more than any other state. The St. Louis disaster is the earliest of Missouri's three, preceding the Tri-State Tornado in 1925 and Joplin in 2011. Illinois figures in two entries, and Missouri shares both. Louisiana and Mississippi, through Natchez and the Amite and Purvis tornado, form the only other pair that turns up together twice.

## Great Natchez Tornado
Illustration: Quartz
The Great Natchez Tornado killed 317 people across Louisiana and Mississippi on May 6, 1840. The Tri-State Tornado alone took more lives among the 10 events. The Natchez storm predates every other entry by decades. The next-oldest disaster, the Great St. Louis Tornado, struck 56 years later in 1896, leaving Natchez as the lone catastrophe from the first half of the 19th century.
Natchez stands apart as the single event with no strength estimate. Each of the nine other tornadoes carries a rating of EF-4 or EF-5. The second-deadliest twister in documented U.S. history leaves behind no gauge of its power beyond its human cost. Readers can compare its death count with any other entry, yet they cannot say whether the Natchez winds matched the fury of the EF-5 storms that followed.
The Natchez entry lists 109 injuries, the smallest such figure in the table and a number below its own deaths. Across the other nine events, the injured outnumber the dead. Every remaining entry logged at least 200 wounded, and the agency offers no reason for the reversal. The thin Natchez injury count hints at gaps in what the 1840 record captured.
Louisiana and Mississippi absorbed another deadly tornado 68 years later. The storm that hit Amite and Purvis crossed the same pair of states and claimed fewer than half as many lives. Mississippi appears in three of the 10 entries, a share Missouri alone matches. Natchez marks the earliest of the three Mississippi disasters, the first sign of a risk the state would face again.
The recorded death count may understate the real loss. Tallies of the dead in Natchez left out enslaved people. Their exclusion points to a higher true toll.
An incomplete roster of victims and an unmeasured force leave much of the oldest storm on the list beyond what its surviving papers can show.

From March 17–18, 1925, one of the deadliest tornado outbreaks in recorded history generated at least 12 significant tornadoes and spanned a large portion of the midwestern and southern United States. In all, at least 751 people died, including men, women, and children. 2,298 were injured,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-3) making the outbreak the deadliest tornado outbreak in U.S. history. The outbreak generated several destructive tornadoes in Missouri, Illinois, and Indiana on the same day, as well as significant tornadoes in Alabama and Kansas. In addition to confirmed tornadoes, there were undoubtedly others with lesser impacts, the occurrences of which have been lost to history.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMaddoxGilmoreDoswell_IIIJohns2013-4)
The outbreak included the Tri-State Tornado, the deadliest disaster in Illinois, the deadliest tornado in U.S.

history, and the second-deadliest registered in world history.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-5)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-7) The 219-mile-long (352 km) track left by the tornado, as it crossed from southeastern Missouri, through southern Illinois, and then into southwestern Indiana, is also the longest ever recorded.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJohnsBurgessDoswell_IIIGilmore2013-8) Modern meteorological re-analysis has suggested that the extremely long path length and lifespan reported in historical accounts are perhaps more plausibly attributed to multiple independent tornadoes belonging to a tornado family, rather than a single, continuous tornado.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMaddoxGilmoreDoswell_IIIJohns2013-4) Although not officially rated by NOAA, the Tri-State Tornado is recognized by most experts (such as Tom Grazulis[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGrazulis2001b17-9) and Ted Fujita[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFujita197356%E2%80%9383-10)) as an F5 tornado,

the maximum damage rating issued on the Fujita scale.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGrazulis1993796-11)[[nb 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-Outbreak-13)[[nb 3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-Fujita-19)[[nb 4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-Count-23)
Track of the Tri-State tornado
During a six-year review study of the Tri-State tornado published in 2013, new surface and upper air data was obtained and meteorological reanalysis was utilized, adding significantly to knowledge of the synoptic and even mesoscale background of the event. The late winter to early spring of 1925 was warmer and drier than normal over much of the central United States. There apparently was persistent ridging in the western U.S. with a troughing pattern over the central U.S.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMaddoxGilmoreDoswell_IIIJohns2013-4)

The extratropical cyclone that set the synoptic stage for the outbreak was centered over northwestern Montana at 7:00 a.m. CST (13:00UTC) on March 17. Meanwhile, a diffuse area of surface low pressure was centered near Denver, Colorado, in association with a lee trough. Occluded fronts extended from Hudson Bay southwestward into the northern Plains states and into the lee trough. The synoptic cyclone moved south-southeastward across the mountain states to eastern Colorado. A warm front stretched along the Gulf Coast, separating warm, moist air from cool, showery weather with areas of fog that extended from Texas to the Carolinas. A well-mixed early-season continental tropical (cT) air mass existed over West Texas and northern New Mexico. To the east of this hot, dry air, buoyant maritime tropical (mT) air was advecting from the Gulf of Mexico. Simultaneously, a mid- to upper-level shortwave trough likely approached the northwest coast of the U.S. and moved rapidly through the persistent ridge then digging southeastward across the Great Basin and central Rocky Mountains and emerging in the Plains over Colorado. This initiated a "Colorado low" cyclogenesis.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMaddoxGilmoreDoswell_IIIJohns2013-4)
Surface weather analysis on March 18, showing the low-pressure area at the time of the tornado outbreak

## St. Louis - East St. Louis Tornado
Image source: Wikipedia
The victims of this tornado were 255 people, and more than 1,000 were injured. Nearly 9,000 buildings were damaged or completely destroyed. The number of killed people on May 27, 1896, remains unknown. Many of the bodies were washed into the river and never found. The tornado funnel was about 1 mile wide, and the winds speed reached 80 miles per hour. The main blow fell on St. Louis, the capital of Missouri. The storm also affected neighboring East St. Louis (Illinois).

## Tornado Outbreak in the Southwestern United States
On April 9, 1947, several tornadoes hit the southwestern US states of Texas, Oklahoma, and Kansas. The most destructive was the Glazier-Higgins-Woodward tornado (named for the cities it destroyed). It traveled over 150 miles and killed 181 people along the way, injuring almost a thousand.
The storms first hit the small town of Glazier in Texas. Local news reported two people who were nearby during the tornado strike - the disaster threw them about three miles apart from each other. Glazier was almost completely destroyed, as was most of Higgins. The maximum speed during the tornado outbreak was around 50 miles per hour, and the average width of the funnel reached 1.2 miles.

## Conclusion
Though most of the tornadoes described above happened a long time ago, devastating storms still happen in the United States and around the world. Here are the three key steps that will allow you to stay safe during these natural disasters:
1.   Be prepared. Collect an emergency kit consisting of water, medication, and food. Be sure to have access to the Internet, the Weather Channel, and the National Weather Service alerts. Activate those alerts in the RainViewer app so you can receive them directly on your smartphone.  
2.   Watch the weather conditions. If you notice such unusual weather conditions as the dark or green sky, low-lying clouds, roaring sounds, or large hail, take cover immediately.  
3.   Know where the nearest shelter is. If you have a basement in your house, it is the best place to hide.
Stay safe and do not ignore the alerts!

Thunderstorms develop in warm, moist air in advance of eastward- moving cold fronts. These thunderstorms often produce hail, strong winds, and tornadoes. A tornado is a violent rotating column of air extending from a thunderstorm to the ground. The damage from a tornado is a result of the high wind speeds and wind-blown debris.
**Tornadoes can and do occur at any time of the year**, although peak tornado frequency in Illinois is between April and June. Tornadoes tend to occur in the afternoons and evenings with 50% occurring between 3 p.m. and 7 p.m. Illinois averaged 54 tornadoes per year based on the 1991-2020 data.
texts.1:
## How do tornadoes form?
Before thunderstorms develop, a change in wind direction and an increase in wind speed with increasing height creates an invisible, horizontal spinning effect in the lower atmosphere. Rising air within the thunderstorm updraft tilts the rotating air from horizontal to vertical. An area of rotation, 2 to 6 miles wide, now extends through much of the storm. Most strong and violent tornadoes form within this area of strong rotation. The newer National Weather Service Doppler radar can detect these areas of rotation, leading to an earlier warning time.
Illustration of the basic steps of tornado formation. Image source: NOAA SciJinks (https://www.nesdis.noaa.gov/about/k-12-education/severe-weather/what-causes-tornadoes).
texts.2:
## Tornado Facts
*   Tornadoes can be almost invisible, marked only by swirling debris at the base of the funnel. Some are composed of several mini-funnels.  
*   On average, the United States experiences 100,000 thunderstorms per year. About 1,000 tornadoes develop from these storms.  
*   The prime tornado period in Illinois is April through June, with 63% of Illinois’ tornadoes occurring during that time.  
*   Average number of tornadoes in Illinois is 54 per year, but there were none in 1919 and 1933, and as many as 124 tornadoes in 2006 and 121 in 2023.  
*   Illinois has experienced two of the worst tornadoes in the nation’s history: the infamous Tri-State tornado of March 18, 1925, which resulted in 695 deaths, 2000 injuries, and $130 million in property damage; and the Mattoon tornado of May 26, 1917, which resulted in 101 deaths, 638 injuries, and $55 million in property damage.  
*   Damage to buildings is caused by violent winds and debris slamming into the building, not by the low pressure of the tornado as it passes overhead.

****
The plot above shows the frequency of tornadoes in Illinois by month between 1950 and 2020. About 64 percent of tornadoes over that time occurred between April and June; however, tornadoes do occur outside of this time. For example, between 1950 and 2020 more tornadoes occurred in December and February together than in September and October together.
This plot shows the number of tornado-related fatalities by month for Illinois. April is the deadliest month with 97 reported deaths, mostly due to the 58 deaths associated with the 1967 Oak Lawn tornado outbreak. The second deadliest month was August, mostly due to the 29 deaths associated with the August 28, 1990, Plainfield event.
Importantly, December and February are the 4th and 5th deadliest months in Illinois despite have the 4th and 5th fewest tornadoes, respectively.

## First Radar-Detected Tornado
The first documented case of atornado being detected by radaroccurred near Champaign, Illinois. On April 9, 1953, while running tests on a research radar unit after hours, Don Staggs of the Illinois State Water Survey discovered an interesting radar return and began recording it using a 35mm camera. As a result, he was able to document the development, growth, and movement of a tornado, as identified by the distinctive “hook echo.” This was later correlated with damage reports from the area. This discovery helped in push for a nationwide network of radar sites in the 1950s to spot and track tornadoes.

Mississippi appears in three of the 10 entries, matching Missouri and outpacing every other state. The Great Natchez Tornado of 1840 and the Amite and Purvis event of 1908 each also reached Louisiana. Tupelo stands as the only one of the three confined to Mississippi. Spread across 96 years, from 1840 to 1936, those appearances show catastrophic tornadoes returning to the state across generations.
texts.9:
## Great St. Louis Tornado
Illustration: Quartz
The Great St. Louis Tornado killed 255 people and injured 1,000 more on May 27, 1896, as it moved across Missouri and Illinois. Its toll tops the two other EF-4 events in the table, the tornadoes that hit Gainesville and the towns of Amite and Purvis. Five of the six EF-5 storms on the list killed fewer people than this 1896 tornado did. Among the top-rated events, only the Tri-State Tornado took more lives, and its losses ran more than twice as heavy.
The tornado went by a second name, the Great Cyclone, and it cut into the center of St. Louis. Its path ran through the Soulard neighborhood and reached the levee downtown. Along the wharf, the funnel battered steamboats and ferryboats. The twister crossed the Mississippi River and inflicted heavy damage on the eastern approach of the Eads Bridge. From there it pushed into East St. Louis, Illinois, the other state on its listing.
The St. Louis tornado's injury count equals the one Joplin recorded in 2011, more than a century later. Only two entries wounded more people, the Tri-State Tornado and the Gainesville storm. No EF-5 event besides the Tri-State Tornado hurt more people than the 1896 storm. The 1896 tornado came 29 years before any of the three other events with four-digit injury tolls.
Only the 1840 Natchez tornado predates this one, and with Natchez unrated, the St. Louis twister stands as the oldest event in the table to carry an intensity estimate. Missouri and Mississippi each appear in three entries, more than any other state. The St. Louis disaster is the earliest of Missouri's three, preceding the Tri-State Tornado in 1925 and Joplin in 2011. Illinois figures in two entries, and Missouri shares both. Louisiana and Mississippi, through Natchez and the Amite and Purvis tornado, form the only other pair that turns up together twice.
texts.10:
## Great Natchez Tornado
Illustration: Quartz
The Great Natchez Tornado killed 317 people across Louisiana and Mississippi on May 6, 1840. The Tri-State Tornado alone took more lives among the 10 events. The Natchez storm predates every other entry by decades. The next-oldest disaster, the Great St. Louis Tornado, struck 56 years later in 1896, leaving Natchez as the lone catastrophe from the first half of the 19th century.
Natchez stands apart as the single event with no strength estimate. Each of the nine other tornadoes carries a rating of EF-4 or EF-5. The second-deadliest twister in documented U.S. history leaves behind no gauge of its power beyond its human cost. Readers can compare its death count with any other entry, yet they cannot say whether the Natchez winds matched the fury of the EF-5 storms that followed.
The Natchez entry lists 109 injuries, the smallest such figure in the table and a number below its own deaths. Across the other nine events, the injured outnumber the dead. Every remaining entry logged at least 200 wounded, and the agency offers no reason for the reversal. The thin Natchez injury count hints at gaps in what the 1840 record captured.
Louisiana and Mississippi absorbed another deadly tornado 68 years later. The storm that hit Amite and Purvis crossed the same pair of states and claimed fewer than half as many lives. Mississippi appears in three of the 10 entries, a share Missouri alone matches. Natchez marks the earliest of the three Mississippi disasters, the first sign of a risk the state would face again.
The recorded death count may understate the real loss. Tallies of the dead in Natchez left out enslaved people. Their exclusion points to a higher true toll.
An incomplete roster of victims and an unmeasured force leave much of the oldest storm on the list beyond what its surviving papers can show.

## St. Louis - East St. Louis Tornado
Image source: Wikipedia
The victims of this tornado were 255 people, and more than 1,000 were injured. Nearly 9,000 buildings were damaged or completely destroyed. The number of killed people on May 27, 1896, remains unknown. Many of the bodies were washed into the river and never found. The tornado funnel was about 1 mile wide, and the winds speed reached 80 miles per hour. The main blow fell on St. Louis, the capital of Missouri. The storm also affected neighboring East St. Louis (Illinois).
texts.11:
## Tornado Outbreak in the Southwestern United States
On April 9, 1947, several tornadoes hit the southwestern US states of Texas, Oklahoma, and Kansas. The most destructive was the Glazier-Higgins-Woodward tornado (named for the cities it destroyed). It traveled over 150 miles and killed 181 people along the way, injuring almost a thousand.
The storms first hit the small town of Glazier in Texas. Local news reported two people who were nearby during the tornado strike - the disaster threw them about three miles apart from each other. Glazier was almost completely destroyed, as was most of Higgins. The maximum speed during the tornado outbreak was around 50 miles per hour, and the average width of the funnel reached 1.2 miles.
texts.12:
## Conclusion
Though most of the tornadoes described above happened a long time ago, devastating storms still happen in the United States and around the world. Here are the three key steps that will allow you to stay safe during these natural disasters:
1.   Be prepared. Collect an emergency kit consisting of water, medication, and food. Be sure to have access to the Internet, the Weather Channel, and the National Weather Service alerts. Activate those alerts in the RainViewer app so you can receive them directly on your smartphone.  
2.   Watch the weather conditions. If you notice such unusual weather conditions as the dark or green sky, low-lying clouds, roaring sounds, or large hail, take cover immediately.  
3.   Know where the nearest shelter is. If you have a basement in your house, it is the best place to hide.
Stay safe and do not ignore the alerts!

Source: https://www.weather.gov/ilx/26may1917
Title: The Mattoon-Charleston Tornado Disaster of May 26, 1917
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8
Overview
Tornado Specifics
Mattoon
Charleston
Stories
lllinois' 3rd deadliest tornado disaster on record occurred on May 26, 1917. On that date, 108 people were killed across central Illinois, almost all in the Mattoon/Charleston area. Injuries totaled approximately 638. (Some confusion and duplication in the hardest hit areas resulted in some victims being double-counted for a time, thus the higher total shown in the _Tribune_ headline in the above graphic.)
Originally, this was believed to be a single tornado with a path 293 miles long, extending from the Mississippi River across from Louisiana, MO, all the way across central portions of Illinois and Indiana, ending near Mount Vernon, IN, over a total time span of 7 hours 20 minutes. This was later determined to be 4 to 8 separate tornadoes; the Illinois portion was approximately 155 miles (including times it was aloft), over a time of approximately 4 hours. The strongest part of the tornado, through Mattoon/Charleston, was later determined to be F4 intensity on the original Fujita scale.

## Regional Overview:
The morning surface map showed low pressure centered in northwest Iowa; this had moved to west central Illinois by evening. Showers and thunderstorms had been reported overnight across central Illinois. The forecast called for additional thunderstorms to develop during the afternoon._(Map courtesy of the NOAA Central Library Data Imaging Project)_
Overall, 383 people were killed over an 8 day period between May 25th and June 1st. At least 73 tornadoes occurred across the Midwest and Southeast U.S. during this time, with 15 that were classified as violent (F4 or F5 strength). The map at right, from the Storm Prediction Center, shows the tornadoes that occurred between May 25-27th.
*   **May 25:**At least 6 tornadoes occurred across the central Plains (5 in Kansas, 1 in Nebraska), killing 24 people. An F5 tornado occurred northwest of Wichita, accounting for most of the deaths.  
*   **May 26:**While most of the deaths and tornadoes this day were associated with the Mattoon-Charleston tornadoes, 3 F4-strength tornadoes occurred in Indiana. There were also tornadoes in northeast Illinois, significantly damaging the village of Manhattan.  
*   **May 27:**Tornadoes affected areas from Missouri and Arkansas eastward into Kentucky, Tennessee, and Alabama. There were 143 deaths, including 67 from an F4 tornado in Kentucky.  
*   **May 28:**Three strong tornadoes occurred in Alabama, killing 8 people.  
*   **May 30:**At least 14 tornadoes occurred in Missouri, killing 65 people. One F3 tornado crossed the Mississippi River into Illinois before ending near Chester.  
*   **May 31:**Severe thunderstorms occurred in Oklahoma and Texas, with an F4 tornado near Marietta, OK.  
*   **June 1:**Tornadoes struck Kentucky, Oklahoma, and Kansas. The strongest tornado of this group, an F4, killed 14 people in Oklahoma.
* * *

## References:
Archives of regional newspapers from 1917 were reviewed to compile this page. The _Mattoon Journal Gazette_, _Decatur Herald_, _Decatur Review_, and _Chicago Tribune_ were most heavily used. Listings of the dead in the newspapers of the time were cross-referenced using cemetery records (specifically the Dodge Grove Cemetery and Find-a-Grave websites) and the statewide death index from the Illinois state archives. This resulted in a few adjustments to the casualty total from other references regarding this event.
Other references include:

## References:
*   _Significant Tornadoes, 1680-1991_, by Thomas Grazulis, published in 1993.  
*   The Central Illinois Tornado of May 26, 1917, by J.P. Carey, appearing in the journal _Geographical Review_, Vol. 4, Issue 2 (Aug. 1917). An abbreviated version of this article also appeared in the journal _Science_, Vol. 45, No. 1172 (June 15, 1917).  
*   _C_ _limatological Data_, published by the U.S. Weather Bureau, May 1917 edition.  
*   The Tornadoes and Windstorms of May 25-June 6, 1917, by H.C. Frankenfield, appearing in the journal _Monthly Weather Review_, Vol. 45, No. 6 (June 1917).  
*   _Illinois Tornadoes_, published by by John W. Wilson and Stanley A. Changnon Jr. of the Illinois State Water Survey in 1971.  
*   Temporal Aspects of Illinois Tornadoes, 1950-1998, by James R. Angel of the Illinois State Water Survey, appearing in _Transactions of the Illinois State Academy of Sciences_(2002), Vol. 95, No. 3.  
*   GenDisasters homepage  
*   Coles County Legal History Project homepage, Eastern Illinois University  
*   _Nature's Fury and the Human Spirit_, a documentary by Cameron Craig and William Lovekamp of Eastern Illinois University  
*   Anniversary editions of the _Mattoon Journal Gazette_: May 26, 1967 (50th anniversary),May 26, 1992 (75th anniversary), August 17, 2005 (Mattoon sesquicentennial), May 26, 2007 (90th anniversary)  
*   1917 Coles County Tornado, put together by Coles County Regional Planning
* * *

## Additional Information:
If you have any contributions you would like to make this page, such as photos or stories, please send them to [Chris.Geelhart@noaa.gov](mailto:Chris.Geelhart@noaa.gov?subject=Mattoon%2FCharleston%20Tornado).

## Tornado History:
Intermittent contact with the ground was initially reported, before a steadier track began about 2 miles east of Nebo (southern **Pike County**) around 12:15 pm, where 5 people were injured. The tornado crossed northern **Greene County** and reached White Hall around 1 pm, then it was partially aloft until reaching Modesto, in northwest **Macoupin County**, around 1:30 pm. It crossed the narrow portion of **Montgomery County** northeast of Farmersville, then entered southern **Christian County**. It was partially aloft before touching down again west of Owaneco around 2:20 pm. Continuing on a nearly due east track and continuously on the ground, the tornado entered **Shelby County** and struck Westervelt at 2:50 pm. It crossed into far southern **Moultrie County** before entering **Coles County**. The tornado entered Mattoon around 3:25 pm, and after lifting for a brief time around Loxa, it reached Charleston around 3:45 pm. The most severe damage (and highest death toll) occurred in Mattoon and Charleston. Toward the end of the track, it curved northeast and dissipated near the town of Embarras; another tornado formed 5 miles southeast of Charleston and tracked southeast through **Clark County**, causing significant damage near Westfield and Marshall.
Click on the images below for an approximate track through each of these counties. The track maps were adapted from work by Wilson and Chagnon (1971) and Grazulis (1993).

## Highlights Along the Track:
**Time****Location****Casualties****Damage**  
1 PM White Hall
(Greene County)3 injured Damage to farm properties  
1:30 PM Modesto
(Macoupin County)3 killed, 20 injured 30 homes destroyed, 35 badly damaged. Business district largely destroyed.  
2:20 PM Owaneco
(Christian County)1 killed Many barns damaged or destroyed  
2:50 PM Westervelt
(Shelby County)6 killed, 25 injured 10 homes and a church destroyed, 9 badly damaged.  
3:25 PM Mattoon
(Coles County)64 killed, 467 injured 496 houses destroyed and 143 partially destroyed, leaving 2,500 homeless.
Nearly every home in the northern half of town was damaged or destroyed.
Near total destruction in a swath 2.5 miles long by 2.5 blocks wide.
Damage estimates $1.3 million (1917 dollars).  
3:45 PM Charleston
(Coles County)34 killed, 182 injured 221 homes destroyed and another 265 seriously damaged.
Damage swath 1.5 miles long by 600 yards wide.
Damage estimates $1 million (1917 dollars).
The Mattoon/Charleston portion of the tornado track was surveyed by Clarence J. Root, the meteorologist in charge of the Weather Bureau office in Springfield. According to his report from the May 1917 edition of _Climatological Data_(shown on the last page at this link), the appearance of the tornado(es) changed over the course of the track:

## Highlights Along the Track:
_Across the State from the Mississippi River almost to Mattoon, all eye witnesses agree that the storm had the typical funnel-shaped tornado cloud with the swinging tail, and east of Charleston the same type of cloud was reported, but the writer, who visited Mattoon and Charleston, failed to find anyone in those cities who saw a funnel-shaped cloud. Eye witnesses who were near the edge of the city, and had an unobstructed view, agree that the approaching storm appeared as a low, boiling mass of clouds, one part a little to the north and the other a little to the south. The parts seemed to roll toward one another, coming together and downward like the meshing of a pair of cog-wheels. There was an abundance of evidence of true tornadic action, ... it might be suggested that the cloud was so low that there was no room for the usual pendant portion._
According to a June 1st article by the _Decatur Daily Review_, Root spent 3 days surveying the damage. "The wonder to me is that not more people were killed," said Root.
The tornado passed a mile north of the Eastern Illinois Normal School (now Eastern Illinois University) in Charleston. There, barograph traces indicated the barometric pressure fell 0.27 inches, then immediately rose 0.40 inches, as the tornado passed. Winds were estimated to reach 80 mph, and hail of 2-1/4 inches in diameter was measured.
In early days, it was believed that tornado damage was caused by buildings "exploding" from the contrast in pressure. J.P. Carey, of the Department of Geography at the school, wrote the following in the June 15, 1917 edition of the journal _Science_:
_The reason for the location of the area of complete devastation being to the right of the center seems to be plausibly explained when the agents of destruction are considered. On the right of the center there is explosive action due to the reduced pressure on the outside of the buildings, the eastward component of the counter-clockwise wind of the tornado (probably over 400 miles per hour), the forward movement of the storm, and the west wind which was prevalent at that time all working in conjunction as agents of destruction..._

## Highlights Along the Track:
Of course, later research determined that the wind speed in tornadoes does not reach as high as 400 mph, but much was unknown about tornadoes and meteorology in general at the time.
In Mattoon, the tornado arrived around 3:25 pm. Clarence Root, the meteorologist in charge of the Springfield Weather Bureau office, reported that eyewitnesses on the edge of town described the storm as a "low, boiling mass of clouds" with no funnel clearly visible. However, according to the June 4th edition of the _Mattoon Journal Gazette_, one witness about 3 miles north of town described seeing "3 distinct funnels," and several other witnesses indicated two storm centers seemed to merge. (It is possible this may have been a multi-vortex tornado, but not enough evidence exists to make such a determination.)
The northern half of the town (largely everything north of DeWitt Ave.) was severely affected, with nearly every home damaged or destroyed in a swath 2.5 miles long by 2.5 blocks wide. A total of 496 houses were totally destroyed, and 143 were severely damaged, with damage estimates around $1.3 million (in 1917 dollars). Survey results indicated that this particular part of town consisted of cottages or small dwellings with no basements. The tornado struck a lumberyard, and flying wood from it struck a number of people that were caught outside.The main business district was largely unscathed by the storm, but did have broken windows and some tree damage. However, the T.W. Clark Manufacturing company was severely damaged, with damage estimates at $200,000. The storm also impacted Dodge Grove Cemetery (ironically, the final resting place of many of the tornado victims), overturning hundreds of grave markers and demolishing a mausoleum. However, the dwelling of the cemetery sexton remained standing, although significantly damaged.
The _Journal Gazette_, in the May 28th edition, noted that the tornado occurred one day before the anniversary of the 1896 St. Louis-East St. Louis tornado, which killed 255 people (140 in Illinois).

## Tornado History:
Intermittent contact with the ground was initially reported, before a steadier track began about 2 miles east of Nebo (southern **Pike County**) around 12:15 pm, where 5 people were injured. The tornado crossed northern **Greene County** and reached White Hall around 1 pm, then it was partially aloft until reaching Modesto, in northwest **Macoupin County**, around 1:30 pm. It crossed the narrow portion of **Montgomery County** northeast of Farmersville, then entered southern **Christian County**. It was partially aloft before touching down again west of Owaneco around 2:20 pm. Continuing on a nearly due east track and continuously on the ground, the tornado entered **Shelby County** and struck Westervelt at 2:50 pm. It crossed into far southern **Moultrie County** before entering **Coles County**. The tornado entered Mattoon around 3:25 pm, and after lifting for a brief time around Loxa, it reached Charleston around 3:45 pm. The most severe damage (and highest death toll) occurred in Mattoon and Charleston. Toward the end of the track, it curved northeast and dissipated near the town of Embarras; another tornado formed 5 miles southeast of Charleston and tracked southeast through **Clark County**, causing significant damage near Westfield and Marshall.
Click on the images below for an approximate track through each of these counties. The track maps were adapted from work by Wilson and Chagnon (1971) and Grazulis (1993).

## Highlights Along the Track:
_Across the State from the Mississippi River almost to Mattoon, all eye witnesses agree that the storm had the typical funnel-shaped tornado cloud with the swinging tail, and east of Charleston the same type of cloud was reported, but the writer, who visited Mattoon and Charleston, failed to find anyone in those cities who saw a funnel-shaped cloud. Eye witnesses who were near the edge of the city, and had an unobstructed view, agree that the approaching storm appeared as a low, boiling mass of clouds, one part a little to the north and the other a little to the south. The parts seemed to roll toward one another, coming together and downward like the meshing of a pair of cog-wheels. There was an abundance of evidence of true tornadic action, ... it might be suggested that the cloud was so low that there was no room for the usual pendant portion._
According to a June 1st article by the _Decatur Daily Review_, Root spent 3 days surveying the damage. "The wonder to me is that not more people were killed," said Root.
The tornado passed a mile north of the Eastern Illinois Normal School (now Eastern Illinois University) in Charleston. There, barograph traces indicated the barometric pressure fell 0.27 inches, then immediately rose 0.40 inches, as the tornado passed. Winds were estimated to reach 80 mph, and hail of 2-1/4 inches in diameter was measured.
In early days, it was believed that tornado damage was caused by buildings "exploding" from the contrast in pressure. J.P. Carey, of the Department of Geography at the school, wrote the following in the June 15, 1917 edition of the journal _Science_:
_The reason for the location of the area of complete devastation being to the right of the center seems to be plausibly explained when the agents of destruction are considered. On the right of the center there is explosive action due to the reduced pressure on the outside of the buildings, the eastward component of the counter-clockwise wind of the tornado (probably over 400 miles per hour), the forward movement of the storm, and the west wind which was prevalent at that time all working in conjunction as agents of destruction..._
texts.8:
## Highlights Along the Track:
Of course, later research determined that the wind speed in tornadoes does not reach as high as 400 mph, but much was unknown about tornadoes and meteorology in general at the time.
In Mattoon, the tornado arrived around 3:25 pm. Clarence Root, the meteorologist in charge of the Springfield Weather Bureau office, reported that eyewitnesses on the edge of town described the storm as a "low, boiling mass of clouds" with no funnel clearly visible. However, according to the June 4th edition of the _Mattoon Journal Gazette_, one witness about 3 miles north of town described seeing "3 distinct funnels," and several other witnesses indicated two storm centers seemed to merge. (It is possible this may have been a multi-vortex tornado, but not enough evidence exists to make such a determination.)
The northern half of the town (largely everything north of DeWitt Ave.) was severely affected, with nearly every home damaged or destroyed in a swath 2.5 miles long by 2.5 blocks wide. A total of 496 houses were totally destroyed, and 143 were severely damaged, with damage estimates around $1.3 million (in 1917 dollars). Survey results indicated that this particular part of town consisted of cottages or small dwellings with no basements. The tornado struck a lumberyard, and flying wood from it struck a number of people that were caught outside.The main business district was largely unscathed by the storm, but did have broken windows and some tree damage. However, the T.W. Clark Manufacturing company was severely damaged, with damage estimates at $200,000. The storm also impacted Dodge Grove Cemetery (ironically, the final resting place of many of the tornado victims), overturning hundreds of grave markers and demolishing a mausoleum. However, the dwelling of the cemetery sexton remained standing, although significantly damaged.
The _Journal Gazette_, in the May 28th edition, noted that the tornado occurred one day before the anniversary of the 1896 St. Louis-East St. Louis tornado, which killed 255 people (140 in Illinois).

On This Day – May 26, 1917
One of the deadliest and longest-tracked tornadoes in U.S. history tore through the Midwest on this day in 1917.
An estimated F4 tornado touched down near Louisiana, Missouri, and tore a path across three states—traveling nearly 300 miles before dissipating in Indiana. It devastated the towns of Mattoon and Charleston, Illinois, killing 101 people and injuring over 600.
At its peak, the tornado was nearly 2.5 miles wide, leaving behind a scene of unimaginable destruction. Homes were leveled. Railcars thrown. Entire neighborhoods erased.
Whether it was one massive tornado or a series of powerful twisters, the outcome was the same—a scar etched into the heart of the Midwest.

This devastating and long-tracked tornado event first began before noon CST in eastern Missouri,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-IL1-6) where significant hail was reported,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-ClimIL-8) then crossed the Mississippi River into Illinois near Pleasant Hill.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-Carey-7) These two towns were probably hit by two separate, weak tornadoes which formed from the same thunderstorm, but intense tornado damage only began 2 miles (3.2 km) east of Nebo, Illinois.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-Grazulis2-9) From there, moving east at about 40 miles per hour (64km/h),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-MWR1-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-Carey-7) the first violent member of the event moved into White Hall,

## Meteorological synopsis
### Mattoon/Charleston, Illinois
hitting farms and injuring six people[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-ClimIL-8) before weakening and dissipating.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-Grazulis2-9) Another tornado probably developed over Modesto, 22 miles (35 km) to the east.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-ClimIL-8) In Modesto, the tornado destroyed 30 homes and damaged 35 others, with three deaths, 16 injuries, and $120,000 damage reported.
Over the next 50 miles (80 km), the tornado either weakened or lifted before touching down again at Dunkel, destroying many homes and barns,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-ClimIL-8) and continuing into Westervelt.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-Grazulis2-9) It destroyed 10 homes and killed four people in Westervelt, but much of the damage was due to hail. Rural areas between Dunkel and Westervelt reportedly received severe damage and reported one death.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-ClimIL-8)

## Meteorological synopsis
### Mattoon/Charleston, Illinois
After hitting Westervelt, the tornado weakened and probably lifted before reforming and re-intensifying[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-Grazulis2-9) over southern Moultrie County.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-ClimIL-8) The new tornado then passed directly through the northern half of Mattoon, causing F4 damage and "near-total destruction" in its path.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-Grazulis2-9) It destroyed 496 homes, damaged 284, and killed at least 53 people in Mattoon; in the hardest-hit areas, few walls were left standing and only small debris remained.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-ClimIL-8) Total damage in Mattoon reached $1.2 million.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-Grazulis2-9) Between Mattoon and Charleston, a distance of 11 miles (18 km), all farms registered damage and often lost buildings.

## [PDF page 8]
On a national scale the 695 deaths from the Tri-State tornado represent almost  
8  percent  of  all  tornado  deaths  registered  since  1915.  The  occurrence  of  a  single  
tornado caused Linehan (1957) to include southern Illinois in his area of prime  
tornado  death  threat.
Illinois  has  a  higher  tornado-death  total  than  any  other  state  and  ranks  sec-  
ond  in  property  loss.  Of  the  1033  people  killed  in  Illinois  by  tornadoes  since  
1915,  606  were  killed  by  the  Tri-State  tornado.  Thus,  a  single  hour  out  of  
447,000 hours in the 1916-1969 period experienced enough deaths to make Illinois  
more  than  40  years  later  still  rank  as  the  state  with  most  tornado  deaths.  The  
Illinois damage produced by the Tri-State tornado represents 23 percent of the  
total  unadjusted  national  losses  in  the  1916-1965  period.  Again,  a  single  tornado  
is a major reason for the high national position the state achieves in property  
damages.  It  is  worthy  of  mention  that  another  long-path  Illinois  tornado  in  1917  
produced 101 deaths and $2.5 million in losses, showing the extreme concentration  
of  state  losses  during  the  early  portion  of  this  century.

## [PDF page 8]
In  the  1916-1969  period  Illinois  has  had  293  tornado  days,  and  one  of  these,  
or 0.34 percent, produced 59 percent of the deaths and 23 percent of the property  
damages.  The  effect  of  this  one  storm  on  national  and  state  tornado  statistics  
reveals  the  'skewness'  caused  by  only  one  such  sample  in  current  climatological  
data.

Shows tornado frequency by year with both actual annual counts (bars) and a 5-year moving average (line) to reveal long-term trends. The moving average helps smooth out year-to-year variations, making it easier to identify patterns and changes over time.

### Tornado Analysis and Trends
#### Property Damage Trends ($ Millions)
Visualizes the financial impact of tornadoes over time with both actual yearly damage (bars) and a 5-year moving average (line) to reveal trends. Toggle between logarithmic and linear scales to view the data in different ways—log scale helps compare years with vastly different damage amounts, while linear scale shows absolute differences more clearly.
**Note:** Property damage data is only available from 1950 onwards. Historical tornado records (1680-1949) do not include damage estimates.
*   Property Damage

The cumulative economic impact of tornadoes in this region is approximately $1.0M. Recent decades show property damage 39 times higher than earlier periods, reflecting changes in both tornado intensity and increased property values in affected areas.

### Tornado Analysis and Trends
#### Tornado Intensity Distribution
Shows the breakdown of tornadoes by intensity rating (EF/F scale). Vertical bars make it easy to compare the prevalence of different tornado strengths, with counts and percentages displayed above each bar.
**Summary:** In MOULTRIE County, Illinois, EF1 tornadoes are the most common, comprising 31.3% of all recorded events. Weak tornadoes (EF0-EF1) account for 56.3% of all events, while strong tornadoes (EF2-EF3) make up 25.1%. Violent tornadoes (EF4-EF5) are relatively rare at only 6.3% of all events, but cause disproportionate damage and casualties.
Note: 12.5% of tornadoes have unknown intensity (FU), typically from historical records where damage assessments were not available.

#### Casualties by Tornado Intensity

This reveals the exponentially increasing danger as tornado strength increases—an EF3 tornado is many times more likely to cause casualties than an EF0 or EF1.Note: Combines historical F-scale (pre-2007) with modern EF-scale (2007+) data.

On This Day – May 26, 1917
One of the deadliest and longest-tracked tornadoes in U.S. history tore through the Midwest on this day in 1917.
An estimated F4 tornado touched down near Louisiana, Missouri, and tore a path across three states—traveling nearly 300 miles before dissipating in Indiana. It devastated the towns of Mattoon and Charleston, Illinois, killing 101 people and injuring over 600.
At its peak, the tornado was nearly 2.5 miles wide, leaving behind a scene of unimaginable destruction. Homes were leveled. Railcars thrown. Entire neighborhoods erased.
Whether it was one massive tornado or a series of powerful twisters, the outcome was the same—a scar etched into the heart of the Midwest.

## Meteorological synopsis
### Mattoon/Charleston, Illinois
hitting farms and injuring six people[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-ClimIL-8) before weakening and dissipating.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-Grazulis2-9) Another tornado probably developed over Modesto, 22 miles (35 km) to the east.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-ClimIL-8) In Modesto, the tornado destroyed 30 homes and damaged 35 others, with three deaths, 16 injuries, and $120,000 damage reported.
Over the next 50 miles (80 km), the tornado either weakened or lifted before touching down again at Dunkel, destroying many homes and barns,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-ClimIL-8) and continuing into Westervelt.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-Grazulis2-9) It destroyed 10 homes and killed four people in Westervelt, but much of the damage was due to hail. Rural areas between Dunkel and Westervelt reportedly received severe damage and reported one death.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-ClimIL-8)

## Meteorological synopsis
### Mattoon/Charleston, Illinois
After hitting Westervelt, the tornado weakened and probably lifted before reforming and re-intensifying[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-Grazulis2-9) over southern Moultrie County.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-ClimIL-8) The new tornado then passed directly through the northern half of Mattoon, causing F4 damage and "near-total destruction" in its path.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-Grazulis2-9) It destroyed 496 homes, damaged 284, and killed at least 53 people in Mattoon; in the hardest-hit areas, few walls were left standing and only small debris remained.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-ClimIL-8) Total damage in Mattoon reached $1.2 million.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence_of_May_25_%E2%80%93_June_1,_1917#cite_note-Grazulis2-9) Between Mattoon and Charleston, a distance of 11 miles (18 km), all farms registered damage and often lost buildings.

Source: https://stateclimatologist.isws.illinois.edu/climate-of-illinois/tornadoes-in-illinois/
Title: Tornadoes in Illinois | Illinois State Climatologist | Illinois State Water Survey | Prairie Research Institute
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7
Thunderstorms develop in warm, moist air in advance of eastward- moving cold fronts. These thunderstorms often produce hail, strong winds, and tornadoes. A tornado is a violent rotating column of air extending from a thunderstorm to the ground. The damage from a tornado is a result of the high wind speeds and wind-blown debris.
**Tornadoes can and do occur at any time of the year**, although peak tornado frequency in Illinois is between April and June. Tornadoes tend to occur in the afternoons and evenings with 50% occurring between 3 p.m. and 7 p.m. Illinois averaged 54 tornadoes per year based on the 1991-2020 data.

## How do tornadoes form?
Before thunderstorms develop, a change in wind direction and an increase in wind speed with increasing height creates an invisible, horizontal spinning effect in the lower atmosphere. Rising air within the thunderstorm updraft tilts the rotating air from horizontal to vertical. An area of rotation, 2 to 6 miles wide, now extends through much of the storm. Most strong and violent tornadoes form within this area of strong rotation. The newer National Weather Service Doppler radar can detect these areas of rotation, leading to an earlier warning time.
Illustration of the basic steps of tornado formation. Image source: NOAA SciJinks (https://www.nesdis.noaa.gov/about/k-12-education/severe-weather/what-causes-tornadoes).

## Tornado Facts
*   Tornadoes can be almost invisible, marked only by swirling debris at the base of the funnel. Some are composed of several mini-funnels.  
*   On average, the United States experiences 100,000 thunderstorms per year. About 1,000 tornadoes develop from these storms.  
*   The prime tornado period in Illinois is April through June, with 63% of Illinois’ tornadoes occurring during that time.  
*   Average number of tornadoes in Illinois is 54 per year, but there were none in 1919 and 1933, and as many as 124 tornadoes in 2006 and 121 in 2023.  
*   Illinois has experienced two of the worst tornadoes in the nation’s history: the infamous Tri-State tornado of March 18, 1925, which resulted in 695 deaths, 2000 injuries, and $130 million in property damage; and the Mattoon tornado of May 26, 1917, which resulted in 101 deaths, 638 injuries, and $55 million in property damage.  
*   Damage to buildings is caused by violent winds and debris slamming into the building, not by the low pressure of the tornado as it passes overhead.

## Tornado Data & Accounts for Illinois
**Recent Tornado Data**
Searchable tornado data from other past years is available through the NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information.
**Some Noteworthy Illinois Tornado Events**
*   The record-setting2006 tornado season  
*   National Weather Service accountof the March 18, 1925 Tri-State Tornado  
*   National Weather Service accountof the May 26, 1917, Mattoon Tornado  
*   National Weather Service listof significant Chicago-area tornadoes.
**Tornado Seasonality**
****
The plot above shows the frequency of tornadoes in Illinois by month between 1950 and 2020. About 64 percent of tornadoes over that time occurred between April and June; however, tornadoes do occur outside of this time. For example, between 1950 and 2020 more tornadoes occurred in December and February together than in September and October together.
This plot shows the number of tornado-related fatalities by month for Illinois. April is the deadliest month with 97 reported deaths, mostly due to the 58 deaths associated with the 1967 Oak Lawn tornado outbreak. The second deadliest month was August, mostly due to the 29 deaths associated with the August 28, 1990, Plainfield event.
Importantly, December and February are the 4th and 5th deadliest months in Illinois despite have the 4th and 5th fewest tornadoes, respectively.

## Tornado Plots for Illinois
Using tornado statistics provided by the National Climatic Data Center, here we explore the relationship of selected tornado characteristics with hour of the day, month of the year, from year to year, etc. This was part of a Capstone project by Michael Patrick, a senior (2011) in the Department of Atmospheric Science at the University of Illinois. Nearly all the plots have been updated through 2020. Click any plot to enlarge.

## First Radar-Detected Tornado
The first documented case of atornado being detected by radaroccurred near Champaign, Illinois. On April 9, 1953, while running tests on a research radar unit after hours, Don Staggs of the Illinois State Water Survey discovered an interesting radar return and began recording it using a 35mm camera. As a result, he was able to document the development, growth, and movement of a tornado, as identified by the distinctive “hook echo.” This was later correlated with damage reports from the area. This discovery helped in push for a nationwide network of radar sites in the 1950s to spot and track tornadoes.

Tornadoes frequently occur in Illinois with numbers that are comparable to those in “tornado alley” in the Great Plains. Here are maps showing the geographic distribution of tornadoes across Illinois, each county, and the Midwest for 1950-2010. The data were obtained from NOAA’s Storm Prediction Center and mapped using ArcGIS.

Title: The 10 deadliest tornadoes in U.S. history killed from 116 to 695 people each
Chunks: 7,8,9,10
## Gainesville tornado
Illustration: Quartz
An EF-4 tornado that hit Gainesville, Georgia, on April 6, 1936, killed 203 people and injured 1,600 more. Among the 10 events on the list, only the Tri-State Tornado of 1925 left more people hurt. Georgia appears nowhere else in the table, which leaves this storm as the state's sole entry.
Gainesville's wounded outnumber those of every EF-5 storm in the table except Tri-State. The Georgia tornado carried an EF-4 estimate, one step below Joplin, Woodward$WWD -1.90%, and Flint, yet it harmed at least 600 more people than any of the three.
Gainesville also surpassed the two other EF-4 entries, the Great St. Louis Tornado and the Amite and Purvis tornado, in injuries. A lower intensity estimate did not cap how many people a storm on this list would harm. The table offers no reason for the gap, but it shows that a storm's estimated strength and its human toll did not rise in step.
Gainesville recorded about eight injuries for every death, the steepest such ratio in the table. Flint comes nearest at a little more than seven, and Joplin follows at about six. Tri-State, with far larger totals, left fewer than three injured for each person killed. Close to nine in 10 of the Georgia storm's recorded casualties survived.
Gainesville's 1,803 combined dead and injured trail only Tri-State's 2,722. No other event reached 1,300, including the Woodward Tornado, which crossed three states, and the Great St. Louis Tornado, which crossed two. A storm the table assigns to a single state outdid both. A multistate path on this list did not guarantee the heavier human cost.
Gainesville's combined toll also exceeds those of the Great Natchez Tornado, the Great St. Louis Tornado, and the Tupelo tornado, all three of which killed more people. A ranking built on deaths alone understates how many lives the Georgia storm upended.

## Tupelo tornado
Illustration: Quartz
An EF-5 tornado killed 216 people in Tupelo, Mississippi, on April 5, 1936, a toll that holds fourth place among the country's deadliest documented twisters. Of the six storms on the list carrying an EF-5 estimate, only the Tri-State Tornado claimed more lives. No event confined to a single state killed more people than the Tupelo storm. The Gainesville, Joplin, New Richmond, and Flint storms each hit one state, and each left a smaller death count. Tupelo's figure exceeds Joplin's by 58 deaths, a gap separating two EF-5 strikes 75 years apart.
Tupelo recorded 700 injuries, the second-smallest figure among the EF-5 entries and above only New Richmond's in Wisconsin. The Mississippi storm produced about 3.2 injuries per death, a lower ratio than six of the other nine events on the list. Only the Tri-State, Great Natchez, and New Richmond tornadoes left fewer wounded for each person killed. Tupelo's deaths weighed heavier against its injuries than at most other sites on the list.
Gainesville, Georgia, faced its own killer tornado the next day, April 6, 1936. Together, the two strikes on consecutive days claimed 419 lives, more than any single event on the list except the Tri-State Tornado. Their combined 2,300 injuries surpass the figure for every individual entry, Tri-State included. The pair also belongs to a wider April cluster. Four of the 10 events arrived in that month, including the Amite and Purvis storm of 1908 and the 1947 Woodward$WWD -1.90% Tornado, and no other month accounts for more than three.
Mississippi appears in three of the 10 entries, matching Missouri and outpacing every other state. The Great Natchez Tornado of 1840 and the Amite and Purvis event of 1908 each also reached Louisiana. Tupelo stands as the only one of the three confined to Mississippi. Spread across 96 years, from 1840 to 1936, those appearances show catastrophic tornadoes returning to the state across generations.

## Great St. Louis Tornado
Illustration: Quartz
The Great St. Louis Tornado killed 255 people and injured 1,000 more on May 27, 1896, as it moved across Missouri and Illinois. Its toll tops the two other EF-4 events in the table, the tornadoes that hit Gainesville and the towns of Amite and Purvis. Five of the six EF-5 storms on the list killed fewer people than this 1896 tornado did. Among the top-rated events, only the Tri-State Tornado took more lives, and its losses ran more than twice as heavy.
The tornado went by a second name, the Great Cyclone, and it cut into the center of St. Louis. Its path ran through the Soulard neighborhood and reached the levee downtown. Along the wharf, the funnel battered steamboats and ferryboats. The twister crossed the Mississippi River and inflicted heavy damage on the eastern approach of the Eads Bridge. From there it pushed into East St. Louis, Illinois, the other state on its listing.
The St. Louis tornado's injury count equals the one Joplin recorded in 2011, more than a century later. Only two entries wounded more people, the Tri-State Tornado and the Gainesville storm. No EF-5 event besides the Tri-State Tornado hurt more people than the 1896 storm. The 1896 tornado came 29 years before any of the three other events with four-digit injury tolls.
Only the 1840 Natchez tornado predates this one, and with Natchez unrated, the St. Louis twister stands as the oldest event in the table to carry an intensity estimate. Missouri and Mississippi each appear in three entries, more than any other state. The St. Louis disaster is the earliest of Missouri's three, preceding the Tri-State Tornado in 1925 and Joplin in 2011. Illinois figures in two entries, and Missouri shares both. Louisiana and Mississippi, through Natchez and the Amite and Purvis tornado, form the only other pair that turns up together twice.

## Great Natchez Tornado
Illustration: Quartz
The Great Natchez Tornado killed 317 people across Louisiana and Mississippi on May 6, 1840. The Tri-State Tornado alone took more lives among the 10 events. The Natchez storm predates every other entry by decades. The next-oldest disaster, the Great St. Louis Tornado, struck 56 years later in 1896, leaving Natchez as the lone catastrophe from the first half of the 19th century.
Natchez stands apart as the single event with no strength estimate. Each of the nine other tornadoes carries a rating of EF-4 or EF-5. The second-deadliest twister in documented U.S. history leaves behind no gauge of its power beyond its human cost. Readers can compare its death count with any other entry, yet they cannot say whether the Natchez winds matched the fury of the EF-5 storms that followed.
The Natchez entry lists 109 injuries, the smallest such figure in the table and a number below its own deaths. Across the other nine events, the injured outnumber the dead. Every remaining entry logged at least 200 wounded, and the agency offers no reason for the reversal. The thin Natchez injury count hints at gaps in what the 1840 record captured.
Louisiana and Mississippi absorbed another deadly tornado 68 years later. The storm that hit Amite and Purvis crossed the same pair of states and claimed fewer than half as many lives. Mississippi appears in three of the 10 entries, a share Missouri alone matches. Natchez marks the earliest of the three Mississippi disasters, the first sign of a risk the state would face again.
The recorded death count may understate the real loss. Tallies of the dead in Natchez left out enslaved people. Their exclusion points to a higher true toll.
An incomplete roster of victims and an unmeasured force leave much of the oldest storm on the list beyond what its surviving papers can show.

Areas affectedMidwestern and southeastern United States
* * *
Part of the **Tornadoes of 1925**

From March 17–18, 1925, one of the deadliest tornado outbreaks in recorded history generated at least 12 significant tornadoes and spanned a large portion of the midwestern and southern United States. In all, at least 751 people died, including men, women, and children. 2,298 were injured,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-3) making the outbreak the deadliest tornado outbreak in U.S. history. The outbreak generated several destructive tornadoes in Missouri, Illinois, and Indiana on the same day, as well as significant tornadoes in Alabama and Kansas. In addition to confirmed tornadoes, there were undoubtedly others with lesser impacts, the occurrences of which have been lost to history.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMaddoxGilmoreDoswell_IIIJohns2013-4)
The outbreak included the Tri-State Tornado, the deadliest disaster in Illinois, the deadliest tornado in U.S.

history, and the second-deadliest registered in world history.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-5)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-7) The 219-mile-long (352 km) track left by the tornado, as it crossed from southeastern Missouri, through southern Illinois, and then into southwestern Indiana, is also the longest ever recorded.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJohnsBurgessDoswell_IIIGilmore2013-8) Modern meteorological re-analysis has suggested that the extremely long path length and lifespan reported in historical accounts are perhaps more plausibly attributed to multiple independent tornadoes belonging to a tornado family, rather than a single, continuous tornado.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMaddoxGilmoreDoswell_IIIJohns2013-4) Although not officially rated by NOAA, the Tri-State Tornado is recognized by most experts (such as Tom Grazulis[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGrazulis2001b17-9) and Ted Fujita[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFujita197356%E2%80%9383-10)) as an F5 tornado,

the maximum damage rating issued on the Fujita scale.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGrazulis1993796-11)[[nb 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-Outbreak-13)[[nb 3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-Fujita-19)[[nb 4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-Count-23)
Track of the Tri-State tornado
During a six-year review study of the Tri-State tornado published in 2013, new surface and upper air data was obtained and meteorological reanalysis was utilized, adding significantly to knowledge of the synoptic and even mesoscale background of the event. The late winter to early spring of 1925 was warmer and drier than normal over much of the central United States. There apparently was persistent ridging in the western U.S. with a troughing pattern over the central U.S.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMaddoxGilmoreDoswell_IIIJohns2013-4)

The extratropical cyclone that set the synoptic stage for the outbreak was centered over northwestern Montana at 7:00 a.m. CST (13:00UTC) on March 17. Meanwhile, a diffuse area of surface low pressure was centered near Denver, Colorado, in association with a lee trough. Occluded fronts extended from Hudson Bay southwestward into the northern Plains states and into the lee trough. The synoptic cyclone moved south-southeastward across the mountain states to eastern Colorado. A warm front stretched along the Gulf Coast, separating warm, moist air from cool, showery weather with areas of fog that extended from Texas to the Carolinas. This initiated a "Colorado low" cyclogenesis.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMaddoxGilmoreDoswell_IIIJohns2013-4)

* * *
Part of the **Tornadoes of 1925**
texts.1:
From March 17–18, 1925, one of the deadliest tornado outbreaks in recorded history generated at least 12 significant tornadoes and spanned a large portion of the midwestern and southern United States. In all, at least 751 people died, including men, women, and children. 2,298 were injured,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-3) making the outbreak the deadliest tornado outbreak in U.S. history. The outbreak generated several destructive tornadoes in Missouri, Illinois, and Indiana on the same day, as well as significant tornadoes in Alabama and Kansas. In addition to confirmed tornadoes, there were undoubtedly others with lesser impacts, the occurrences of which have been lost to history.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMaddoxGilmoreDoswell_IIIJohns2013-4)
The outbreak included the Tri-State Tornado, the deadliest disaster in Illinois, the deadliest tornado in U.S.
texts.2: history, and the second-deadliest registered in world history.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-5)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-7) The 219-mile-long (352 km) track left by the tornado, as it crossed from southeastern Missouri, through southern Illinois, and then into southwestern Indiana, is also the longest ever recorded.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJohnsBurgessDoswell_IIIGilmore2013-8) Modern meteorological re-analysis has suggested that the extremely long path length and lifespan reported in historical accounts are perhaps more plausibly attributed to multiple independent tornadoes belonging to a tornado family, rather than a single, continuous tornado.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMaddoxGilmoreDoswell_IIIJohns2013-4) Although not officially rated by NOAA, the Tri-State Tornado is recognized by most experts (such as Tom Grazulis[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGrazulis2001b17-9) and Ted Fujita[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFujita197356%E2%80%9383-10)) as an F5 tornado,
texts.3:
the maximum damage rating issued on the Fujita scale.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGrazulis1993796-11)[[nb 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-Outbreak-13)[[nb 3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-Fujita-19)[[nb 4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-Count-23)
Track of the Tri-State tornado
During a six-year review study of the Tri-State tornado published in 2013, new surface and upper air data was obtained and meteorological reanalysis was utilized, adding significantly to knowledge of the synoptic and even mesoscale background of the event. The late winter to early spring of 1925 was warmer and drier than normal over much of the central United States. There apparently was persistent ridging in the western U.S. with a troughing pattern over the central U.S.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMaddoxGilmoreDoswell_IIIJohns2013-4)
texts.4:
The extratropical cyclone that set the synoptic stage for the outbreak was centered over northwestern Montana at 7:00 a.m. CST (13:00UTC) on March 17. Meanwhile, a diffuse area of surface low pressure was centered near Denver, Colorado, in association with a lee trough. Occluded fronts extended from Hudson Bay southwestward into the northern Plains states and into the lee trough. The synoptic cyclone moved south-southeastward across the mountain states to eastern Colorado. A warm front stretched along the Gulf Coast, separating warm, moist air from cool, showery weather with areas of fog that extended from Texas to the Carolinas. A well-mixed early-season continental tropical (cT) air mass existed over West Texas and northern New Mexico. To the east of this hot, dry air, buoyant maritime tropical (mT) air was advecting from the Gulf of Mexico. Simultaneously, a mid- to upper-level shortwave trough likely approached the northwest coast of the U.S. and moved rapidly through the persistent ridge then digging southeastward across the Great Basin and central Rocky Mountains and emerging in the Plains over Colorado. This initiated a "Colorado low" cyclogenesis.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_17%E2%80%9318,_1925#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMaddoxGilmoreDoswell_IIIJohns2013-4)
